7 Best Ecommerce Analytics Tools (2026)
Compare the 7 best ecommerce analytics tools for 2026, from behavioral analytics to session replay, and see which fits your online retail team.
Table of Contents
What ecommerce analytics tools measure
Amplitude is the best ecommerce analytics tool for online retail

Adobe Analytics
Comparison table
How to choose an ecommerce analytics tool
Turn shopper behavior into revenue with Amplitude
Frequently asked questions about ecommerce analytics tools
Most online retailers can tell you how many orders they shipped last quarter.
Far fewer can explain why a shopper added three items to a cart, sat on the checkout page for 40 seconds, then left without buying.
Order reports and pageview dashboards describe the outcome, but rarely the behavior behind it.
Ecommerce analytics tools close that gap by tracking every product view, filter, cart action, and purchase as a behavioral event you can segment, funnel, and tie back to revenue.
This guide compares seven ecommerce analytics tools for 2026 and where each fits. Use the links below to jump to a specific tool or to the how-to-choose section.
Browse this guide
Frequently asked questions
Ecommerce analytics tools measure how shoppers behave across a storefront, not just how many transactions closed.
They capture events like product views, searches, filter applications, add-to-cart actions, checkout steps, and completed purchases, then connect those events to customer identity so you can analyze conversion, retention, and lifetime value.
The difference matters because ecommerce funnels are long and leaky.
A shopper might discover a product through a paid ad, browse on mobile, abandon a cart, then return two days later on desktop and convert.
Traffic-level reporting treats those as separate sessions.
Behavioral analytics stitches them into one journey, so you can see where revenue leaks and which cohorts come back to buy again.
Amplitude is the AI analytics platform that unifies behavioral analytics, funnels, retention, experimentation, and session replay in one workflow, which makes it the strongest fit for ecommerce teams that need to connect shopper behavior to revenue.
Instead of stitching together a pageview tool, a heatmap tool, and a testing tool, a retail team can trace a shopper from first product view through checkout, spot where the funnel leaks, replay the sessions that dropped, then run an experiment to fix it, all against the same event data.
For online retail, that end-to-end loop is the point.
You can build a checkout funnel segmented by device, traffic source, or first-purchase cohort, watch conversion by step, and click straight into session replay to see the shoppers who stalled.
Cohort analysis surfaces which channels produce repeat buyers versus one-time discount hunters, so merchandising and paid teams stop targeting the wrong customer.
Key features
Behavioral funnel analysis. Track multi-step checkout and browse-to-buy funnels with Amplitude Analytics , segment conversion by device, campaign, or product category, and see drop-off between every step.
Retention and lifetime value. Measure repeat-purchase behavior and revenue by cohort, so you can tell which channels deliver loyal buyers rather than one-time orders.
Session Replay. Watch real shopper sessions tied to your funnel and event data with Session Replay , jumping from a drop-off point straight to the recordings behind it.
Feature Experimentation. Run A/B tests on product pages, pricing displays, and checkout flows with built-in experimentation, then read results against the same behavioral metrics.
AI Agents. Ask questions in plain language and get charts back, so a merchandiser can query cart-abandonment rate without building a report from scratch.
CLI setup wizard. The Amplitude CLI walks engineers through SDK installation and event instrumentation in the terminal, cutting time from install to first insight.
Because analytics, replay, and experimentation share one dataset, an insight in a funnel becomes a replay to watch and a test to run without exporting data or switching tools.
Amplitude pros and cons
Unified workspace. Analytics, session replay, experimentation, and engagement live together, so ecommerce teams stop stitching point solutions together.
Outcome-focused insights. Every funnel, cohort, and replay connects back to conversion and revenue.
Fast setup. A CLI-based setup wizard plus AI Agents get retail teams from install to first insight quickly.
Generous free tier. Full platform access on the Free plan, which includes 2M events a month, the most generous free tier available.
High skill ceiling. Amplitude's depth means there's a lot to learn if you want to use the full platform. Getting started is fast thanks to the CLI wizard and AI Agents for natural-language queries, but mastering advanced retention and experimentation workflows takes time.
Google Analytics 4 is a free web and app analytics tool that includes an ecommerce reporting suite for tracking product impressions, add-to-cart events, and purchases.
It's the default starting point for most online stores because it's free, integrates with Google Ads, and ships with prebuilt ecommerce reports.
GA4 fits teams that want channel-level attribution and revenue reporting without paying for a dedicated analytics platform.
Enhanced ecommerce events for product views, cart actions, checkout steps, and purchases
Native integration with Google Ads and Search Ads 360 for campaign attribution
Funnel and path exploration reports in the free tier
BigQuery export for raw event data
Google Analytics 4 pros and cons
Free at scale. Free at almost any traffic volume, with tight integration into the Google advertising stack.
Strong attribution. Strong acquisition and channel attribution reporting out of the box.
Sampling limits. Data sampling and thresholding kick in on high-traffic reports, which distorts conversion numbers for larger stores.
Steeper learning curve. The event model and exploration reports are harder to learn than purpose-built product analytics, and there's no session replay.
See a full Amplitude versus Google Analytics comparison for how the two approaches differ on behavioral depth.
Mixpanel is a product analytics tool built around event tracking, funnels, and retention reports, and it works well for ecommerce teams focused on conversion and engagement metrics.
It's lighter to set up than an enterprise suite and gives merchandising and growth teams self-serve funnel and cohort reports.
Mixpanel fits stores that want behavioral analytics without a heavy implementation.
Event-based funnel and retention analysis
Cohort builder for segmenting buyers by behavior
Interactive reports and boards for self-serve exploration
Impact and experiment reporting on top of tracked events
Mixpanel pros and cons
Fast to stand up. Quick to deploy for teams that mainly need funnels, cohorts, and conversion reports.
Approachable interface. Clean UI for non-technical merchandising and growth staff.
No native session replay. You can't watch the sessions behind a funnel drop-off without a separate tool.
Thinner advanced workflows. Experimentation and warehouse-native workflows are lighter than a unified platform, which pushes larger teams toward add-ons.
For a deeper breakdown, see the Amplitude versus Mixpanel comparison .
Contentsquare is a digital experience analytics tool centered on session replay, zone-based heatmaps, and journey analysis for understanding on-page behavior.
It's strong for ecommerce merchandising and UX teams that want to see how shoppers interact with product and category pages.
Contentsquare fits retailers focused on page-level experience rather than cross-session behavioral analytics.
Zone-based heatmaps showing clicks, hovers, and revenue attribution per page element
Session replay with automatic frustration and struggle detection
Journey analysis across product, category, and checkout pages
Merchandising and product-page revenue reporting
Contentsquare pros and cons
Rich on-page data. Heatmaps tie page elements to revenue.
UX friction diagnosis. Strong at diagnosing friction on high-traffic product and checkout pages.
Limited behavioral analysis. Experience analytics is its core strength, so cross-session behavioral analysis, cohorting, and experimentation are less developed.
Enterprise cost. Enterprise pricing and implementation put it out of reach for smaller stores.
See how the tools compare in the Amplitude versus Contentsquare breakdown .
Heap is an autocapture-based product analytics tool, now part of Contentsquare after its 2023 acquisition, that records every user interaction automatically so teams can analyze events they didn't tag in advance.
For ecommerce, retroactive analysis is the draw: you can define a checkout funnel today and analyze historical data because the events were already captured.
Heap fits teams that want event tracking without upfront instrumentation planning.
Autocapture of clicks, form fills, and pageviews without manual tagging
Retroactive event definition and funnel analysis on historical data
Segments and cohorts built on captured behavior
Session replay added through the Contentsquare portfolio
Heap pros and cons
No upfront tagging. Autocapture removes the upfront tagging burden, so teams start analyzing quickly.
Retroactive analysis. You can answer new questions against past behavior.
Noisy data. Autocapture generates noisy event data that needs cleanup and governance before funnels are trustworthy.
Roadmap uncertainty. Product direction now sits inside the Contentsquare portfolio, which adds uncertainty for long-term roadmap planning.
Compare the two directly in the Amplitude versus Heap overview .
Adobe Analytics is an enterprise digital analytics tool, part of Adobe Experience Cloud, built for large retailers that need deep segmentation and integration with Adobe's marketing suite.
It handles high data volumes and complex attribution, and it pairs tightly with Adobe Target and Adobe Experience Manager.
Adobe Analytics fits enterprise ecommerce organizations already standardized on Adobe.
Advanced segmentation and calculated metrics for large data volumes
Attribution modeling across channels and campaigns
Integration with Adobe Target, Experience Manager, and Real-Time CDP
Anomaly detection and contribution analysis
Adobe Analytics pros and cons
Deep segmentation. Flexible segmentation and attribution for high-volume enterprise retailers.
Adobe ecosystem fit. Tight fit for organizations already invested in Adobe Experience Cloud.
Steep learning curve. Heavy implementation, typically requiring dedicated analysts or consultants.
Cost and complexity. Licensing cost and complexity make it a poor fit for mid-market and smaller stores.
Read the Amplitude versus Adobe comparison for how the platforms differ on time-to-insight.
Glassbox is a digital experience analytics tool focused on session replay, struggle detection, and interaction capture across web and mobile.
It records complete sessions and flags friction signals like rage clicks and error loops, which helps ecommerce and support teams diagnose checkout problems.
Glassbox fits retailers whose priority is experience monitoring and struggle analysis rather than behavioral cohorting.
Full session capture and replay across web and mobile apps
Automated struggle and error detection, including rage clicks and form abandonment
Interaction and journey mapping for checkout flows
Compliance-oriented data capture controls
Glassbox pros and cons
Detailed session replay. Automated friction detection for checkout diagnosis.
Compliance controls. Data capture controls suited to regulated industries handling sensitive information.
Limited behavioral analytics. Experience monitoring is the core focus, so behavioral analytics, funnels, and retention cohorting are limited.
Enterprise-oriented. Enterprise pricing and setup make it heavy for smaller ecommerce teams.

Retroactive analysis without tagging

Amplitude's Free plan includes 2M events a month, the most generous free tier available, so growing teams get full platform access before paying.
Technical resources: Autocapture tools like Heap reduce upfront tagging but create governance work later. Amplitude's CLI wizard and AI Agents shorten setup without leaving you with noisy data to clean up.
Depth of analysis: For page-level UX diagnosis, Contentsquare and Glassbox lead on replay and heatmaps. For cross-session behavior, cohorts, and lifetime value, product analytics platforms go deeper.
Integration needs: Adobe fits teams standardized on Experience Cloud, GA4 fits the Google advertising stack, and warehouse-native platforms connect to your existing data infrastructure.
Most of these are point solutions that answer one slice of the question. The practical choice is a single-purpose tool for each job or an integrated platform that connects behavior, replay, and experimentation in one workflow.

Track browse-to-buy behavior with product analytics , replay the sessions behind a drop-off with Session Replay, run A/B tests on checkout with Feature Experimentation, then measure the revenue impact by cohort.
Instead of exporting data between separate tools, your merchandising, growth, and product teams work from one source of truth about shopper behavior. GA4 remains a common free starting point for channel-level reporting, but it lacks behavioral depth and replay.
Is Google Analytics 4 enough for an ecommerce store?
Google Analytics 4 is enough for smaller stores that need channel attribution and basic revenue reporting, and it's free. Larger stores hit data sampling on high-traffic reports and lack session replay, so they typically add a behavioral analytics platform to see cross-session shopper journeys and lifetime value.
What is the difference between ecommerce analytics and web analytics?
Web analytics reports traffic-level metrics like sessions, pageviews, and bounce rate. Ecommerce analytics tracks shopper behavior as events, like add-to-cart and checkout steps, and ties them to customer identity and revenue. That lets you analyze conversion funnels, repeat-purchase cohorts, and lifetime value rather than just traffic.
Do ecommerce analytics tools include session replay?
